subject: biology-hl
about: Original practice questions written for NevaIB from the IB guide's syllabus understandings and the school's unit order. Not IB past-paper questions, not publisher material and not IB markschemes: the marking points are written for self-marking. Organisms, experiments and data in data-response items are invented for practice.

items.stem: Which property is shared by efficient gas exchange surfaces?
choices: Large surface area and thin, moist, permeable surface
Small surface area and a thick, waterproof surface
Few blood vessels and a dry, waxy surface to reduce water loss
A thick layer of muscle around the surface
items.note: Large area, short diffusion distance, moisture and permeability maximise the rate of diffusion.

items.stem: Gases move across the alveolar wall by:
choices: Active transport using ATP
Diffusion down their concentration gradients
Osmosis through aquaporins in the alveolar wall
Exocytosis of gas-filled vesicles
items.note: O₂ diffuses from alveoli into blood; CO₂ in the reverse direction. Ventilation and blood flow maintain the gradients.

choices: The diaphragm relaxes and domes upward, decreasing volume
The internal intercostal muscles contract and the ribs move down
The diaphragm contracts and flattens, increasing thorax volume
Air is pushed in because pressure in the lungs rises
items.note: Increased volume → lower pressure in the lungs → air flows in. Exhalation at rest is mostly passive recoil.

items.stem: Type II pneumocytes secrete surfactant, which:
choices: Kills bacteria that reach the alveoli in inhaled air
Increases the thickness of the alveolar wall for protection
Carries oxygen across the membrane into red blood cells
Reduces surface tension so alveoli do not collapse
items.note: Surfactant lowers the cohesive forces of the water film, preventing alveoli sticking together on exhalation.

choices: The maximum volume of air that can be breathed out
The air remaining in the lungs after maximum exhalation
The total volume of the lungs at full inhalation
The volume of air breathed in or out in a normal breath
items.note: Vital capacity = maximum exhaled after maximum inhalation; residual volume remains in the lungs.

choices: Water to be pumped into the leaf by active transport
Light to enter the mesophyll layer more easily
Diffusion of CO₂ in and O₂ and water vapour out
Sugars to be transported to other parts of the plant
items.note: Stomata are gas exchange pores, controlled by guard cells. Loss of water vapour through them is transpiration.

items.stem: Which change would increase the rate of transpiration?
choices: Higher temperature
Higher humidity
Lower light intensity
Closed stomata
items.note: Warmth increases evaporation and diffusion. High humidity reduces the water vapour gradient; darkness closes stomata.

items.stem: The oxygen dissociation curve of adult haemoglobin is S-shaped because of:
choices: Competition between oxygen and carbon dioxide for the same binding site
Cooperative binding: each O₂ that binds makes the next bind more easily
The haem groups saturating one at a time at equal rates
Myoglobin releasing oxygen to haemoglobin in muscles
items.note: Binding of one O₂ changes the shape of the protein (allosteric), raising affinity of the remaining sites.

items.stem: The Bohr shift moves the oxygen dissociation curve to the right when:
choices: Carbon dioxide concentration falls, as in the alveoli
Temperature falls in resting muscle tissue
Carbon dioxide concentration rises, as in respiring tissues
The pH of the blood rises above its normal value in the lungs
items.note: CO₂ lowers pH; haemoglobin's affinity for O₂ falls, so more O₂ is released where it is needed.

items.stem: Fetal haemoglobin has a higher affinity for oxygen than adult haemoglobin. This allows:
choices: The fetus to release more CO₂ into the amniotic fluid
The mother to load more oxygen in her own lungs
The fetal heart to pump blood faster
Oxygen to pass from the mother's blood to the fetus in the placenta
items.note: At the same pO₂, fetal Hb is more saturated, so O₂ moves from maternal to fetal blood. Its curve lies to the left.

items.stem: A student counts 45 stomata in a field of view of area 0.15 mm². What is the stomatal density?
choices: 300 mm⁻²
30 mm⁻²
items.note: Density = count ÷ area = 45 ÷ 0.15 = 300 stomata per mm².

items.stem: Explain how the structure of the alveolus is adapted for gas exchange.
markscheme: Wall one cell thick (type I pneumocytes), short diffusion distance (1)
Many alveoli give a large surface area (1)
Dense capillary network maintains concentration gradients (1)
Moist lining lets gases dissolve; surfactant prevents collapse (1)
items.tactic: Pair each feature with its effect on diffusion.

items.stem: Describe how a spirometer can be used to measure tidal volume and vital capacity.
markscheme: Subject breathes normally into the spirometer; the height of each trace is the tidal volume (1)
For vital capacity, maximum inhalation followed by maximum exhalation (1)
Volume read from the calibrated trace / repeat for a mean (1)
items.tactic: Method: what the subject does, what is read from the trace.

items.stem: Explain how the Bohr shift helps supply oxygen to actively respiring muscle.
markscheme: CO₂ forms carbonic acid, lowering the pH (1)
Haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen decreases / curve shifts to the right (1)
More oxygen is released (unloaded) at the same pO₂ in the muscle (1)
items.tactic: Cause-and-effect chain: from respiration to unloading.

items.stem:
(Invented data for practice.) Percentage saturation of two invented animals' haemoglobin at different pO₂ (kPa): pO₂ 2 — animal X 20%, animal Y 45%; pO₂ 4 — X 50%, Y 80%; pO₂ 8 — X 88%, Y 96%; pO₂ 12 — X 97%, Y 98%.
(a) Compare the curves of X and Y. (b) Suggest which animal lives at high altitude, with a reason. (c) Calculate the difference in saturation at 4 kPa.
markscheme: (a) Both reach near-full saturation at 12 kPa; Y is more saturated at low pO₂ (curve to the left) (1)
(b) Y: higher affinity lets it load O₂ where pO₂ is low (1)
Example data quoted (e.g. 45% vs 20% at 2 kPa) (1)
items.tactic: Unfamiliar context: find the syllabus idea being tested, quote the data (with units) when you describe a trend, then explain it with that idea. One marking point per linked step.
